**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The first time I held a pen, it felt like holding a key to an infinite door. The ink bled into the page like blood from a wound—raw, unfiltered, alive. I was eight years old, and the world was too big for my hands, but the paper was just right. It didn’t judge. It didn’t flinch when I scribbled *I hate you* in jagged letters after my father forgot, again, to pick me up from school. The page absorbed it all: the anger, the loneliness, the quiet ache of being a child who couldn’t name what she was feeling.

Words have always been my refuge. Not just the ones I write, but the ones I read—the way a sentence can unravel you, or stitch you back together. Once, in a secondhand bookstore, I found a copy of *The Bell Jar* with a note tucked inside: *"This one’s for the girls who feel too much."* I stole it. (I still feel guilty, but not enough to return it.) That book became a lifeline, a proof that someone, somewhere, had felt the same weight pressing down on their chest and survived to write about it.

But words can also be weapons. I learned that in middle school, when a boy called me *fat* in front of the whole cafeteria, and the word stuck to me like tar, thick and suffocating. For years, I measured myself in syllables—*ugly, stupid, unloved*—until I realized the power wasn’t in the words themselves, but in who got to define me. So I started writing my own.

Now, I fill notebooks with half-finished poems, angry manifestos, love letters to strangers I’ll never meet. Sometimes, the words come easy, like water from a tap. Other times, they’re drag out of me, one by one, like teeth. But they always come. Because silence is heavier than any thousand words.

I think about the things I’ve never said. The *I love you* that died on my tongue the night my grandmother passed. The *I’m scared* I swallowed before my first big job interview. The *me too* that lodged in my throat for years. There’s a grave in my chest where all the unsaid things are buried, and sometimes, late at night, I dig them up and let them breath on the page.

Writing is how I make sense of the chaos. It’s how I turn pain into something beautiful, or at least something bearable. When my mother was sick, I wrote her letters I never sent, filling them with memories of her hands kneading dough, her laughter like wind chimes. When my heart was broken, I turned the hurt into metaphors—*like a vase dropped from a high window, I am all sharp edges now.* When the world felt too loud, I crawled into books and came out the other side quieter, softer.

But here’s the thing about words: they’re not just for the writer. They’re for the reader, too. The one who picks up a story and sees themselves in it for the first time. The one who underlines a sentence so hard the page tears, because finally, *finally*, someone gets it. Words are a bridge. A hand reaching out in the dark. A match struck in the void.

I’ve been given 1,000 words here, but the truth is, I could fill a library with the things I want to say. About love and loss. About the way the light looks at 4 a.m. when the world is asleep except for you and your thoughts. About how мы never really know each other, but we try anyway. About the way a song can reduce you to tears because it remembers a version of you that you’ve forgotten.

Maybe that’s why we write—to remember. To say: *I was here. I felt this. I mattered.*

So here’s my offering: a string of words, imperfect and honest. A thousand little beats of a heart that’s still learning how to speak. Maybe they’ll mean something to you. Maybe they won’t. But they meant something to me, and for now, that’s enough.

(And if you’re reading this, thank you. Really. You just made my words matter.)
